competitorFacts.text: ARC Prize named Tufa Labs and its Duck agent the first-place open-source solution for the June 2026 ARC-AGI-3 Milestone 1 prize.

competitorFacts.sourceTitle: Tufa Labs — Duck Harness technical overview
competitorFacts.text: Tufa Labs says its public Duck harness lets an LLM inspect game grids as image and text, write Python in a REPL, and keep context short by evicting older messages. This describes the published Milestone 1 system, not an unverified current submission.
Tufa Labs lists Dries Smit, Isaiah Pressman and Jeroen Cottaar among its AI researchers, with research interests spanning reinforcement learning, self-play and Bayesian methods.

competitorFacts.sourceTitle: Tufa Labs — October 9 public competition post
competitorFacts.text: On October 9, 2026, Tufa Labs described a temporary setback in a public X post and said it remained dedicated to crushing competitors with overwhelming resources and compute.
Yi-Chia Chen’s Kaggle profile lists her as a Competitions Master and a double-degree student at National Taiwan University and Waseda University.

competitorFacts.sourceTitle: Yi-Chia Chen — Eedi third-place solution write-up
competitorFacts.text: Yi-Chia Chen authored a Kaggle write-up for a third-place solution in Eedi — Mining Misconceptions in Mathematics.

competitorFacts.sourceTitle: Yi-Chia Chen — public Kaggle profile and avatar
competitorFacts.text: Yi-Chia Chen’s public Kaggle account is threerabbits. The profile lists she/her pronouns and displays an avatar of two rabbits.
The public roster now lists all seven accounts together under Team Turducken. This confirms the combined entry, not its exact merger time or any new score gain.

competitorFacts.sourceTitle: Separate ARC2 and ARC3 team entries — dated public roster evidence
competitorFacts.text: On 19 October 2026, Mark Barney announced Jack Cole joining ARC Mutants for ARC-AGI-2. The public ARC2 roster lists jcole75, markbarney, scizical and sonphamorg under team 17023174. Team Turducken (ARC-AGI-3 team 15605182) is a separate entry; this announcement does not add Jack to that ARC3 team.
NVIDIA’s December 2025 report identifies Ivan Sorokin and Jean-Francois Puget as NVIDIA researchers who competed as NVARC in the 2025 ARC Prize.
The 2025 NVARC team write-up credits sorokin and cpmpml. Both handles appear in the observed roster of the distinct 2026 NVARC3 entry. This does not establish an affiliation for every current member.

NVIDIA describes the separate 2025 NVARC ARC-AGI-2 solution as using synthetic data generation, test-time training and a fine-tuned 4B model. This is historical background, not a claim about the 2026 NVARC3 agent.
Jean-François Puget’s public GitHub profile identifies him as CPMP and links directly to the Kaggle account cpmpml.
NVIDIA’s author biography describes Jean-Francois Puget as a director and individual contributor whose team advances agentic AI and showcases NVIDIA tools and expertise in Kaggle competitions.
The rostered lukasaichberger Kaggle profile identifies its owner as Lukas Aichberger and links to his research website.
Johannes Kepler University Linz lists Lukas Aichberger at its Institute for Machine Learning and credits him on research about reasoning models and uncertainty evaluation.
Another rostered account, fses91, describes itself on Kaggle only as Florian; the public profile does not establish a surname.
The rostered dwellement0baser Kaggle profile identifies its owner as Mykyta Ielanskyi.

Johannes Kepler University Linz lists Mykyta Ielanskyi at its Institute for Machine Learning. Its research record credits him and Lukas Aichberger together on a 2026 paper about reward redistribution for reasoning models.

competitorFacts.sourceTitle: Lukas Aichberger — own biography and research directions
competitorFacts.text: His own research biography records an AI PhD co-supervised by Sepp Hochreiter and Yarin Gal, work with OATML at Oxford and reasoning/post-training work at Apple.

competitorFacts.sourceTitle: EuroSkills 2016 — official results, Mobile Robotics page 15
competitorFacts.text: EuroSkills 2016 official Mobile Robotics results list Lukas Aichberger and Florian Müller fifth for Austria; this is separate from Kaggle.

competitorFacts.sourceTitle: Artificial Agency Lab — research and ARC-AGI-3 project
competitorFacts.text: Artificial Agency Lab says it built an ARC-AGI-3 agent combining structured grids and image observations with persistent context updates, keeping model weights fixed; it reports an eighth-place June milestone result.

competitorFacts.sourceTitle: Manifund — Artificial Agency ARC-AGI-3 project proposal
competitorFacts.text: A public ARC-AGI-3 project proposal names Richard Csaky as research lead and Côme Chevalier for engineering. The proposal describes an intended curiosity-driven proof of concept, not a verified method of the current Kaggle submission.
Richard Csaky’s Kaggle account published an “ARC-AGI-3 milestone 2 submission” notebook.

competitorFacts.sourceTitle: Artificial Agency Lab — own research and account links
competitorFacts.text: Artificial Agency Lab’s own site links Richard Csaky to @ricsinaruto and its September 30 ARC-AGI-3 submission; its dated historical methods do not identify the method behind the October 14 score event.

discussionThreads.author: ravi20076
discussionThreads.reason: New substantive public extension request and fairness response read in Newest view and verified logged out. Header shows 62 comments; count discrepancies across surfaces remain. Competitor proposals are not organizer policy.
discussionThreads.summary: On October 27, CPMP asks whether a competition extension is being discussed, citing repeated lost submissions. Grigoriy Zatravkin questions claims that all notebooks were affected and argues that reruns alone cannot restore the lost opportunity to learn from scores and adjust agents. Earlier, Huynh asked that affected nonzero scores be considered and Son Pham accepted the fairness point. The latest read Kaggle staff statement remains Cruz’s October 26 broader-investigation/capacity warning; earlier October 24 engineer replies confirm some rescores had begun. No extension decision, complete eligibility policy or new all-clear appears in this focused read.
discussionThreads.title: Scoring 0 possibly due to dataset loading issues

discussionThreads.author: pathik1511
discussionThreads.reason: Root and author follow-ups now verified without login; narrower limit on a previously archived workaround.
discussionThreads.summary: Pathik Patel reports that extending his server-startup allowance recovered a run from zero to about twenty-nine. In now-public follow-ups he concedes the workaround prevents a zero but does not restore gameplay time lost to slow loading. Other participants raise that time-budget concern. This is an attributed recovery claim, not a desk reproduction or universal remedy. His advice to send IDs conflicts with Cruz’s newer request to hold off.

discussionThreads.reason: Root and staff fix verified without login.

Kaggle staff María Cruz replies at October 26 20:14 UTC that the issue has been fixed and the named users should now be able to enter. A resolved entry-access incident, not a change to the final submission deadline.

sections.heading: Fifth in the world. Clear a space.
sections.text:
The Last Dance has earned the spotlight. Fifth on the ARC-AGI-3 public board among nearly 5,000 teams, the four-account entry is still in the thick of the chase. Ahead sits xz’s newly arrived cat; behind, yktori is less than half a point away. Nobody in this part of the hall gets to put their feet up.

There is more to this act than a good name and a dancing emoji. Three members can be named directly: Florian Sestak, Lukas Aichberger and Mykyta Ielanskyi, all with research ties to Johannes Kepler University Linz. The fourth registered account is gklambauer. The cast brings a veteran’s Kaggle silverware, a robotics competition past and an award-winning logic-puzzle paper into the same entry.

And they have already made the field look twice. On October 5, the saved board caught The Last Dance jumping from twenty-sixth to third. On October 16, another advance carried it from seventh back to third. Thursday’s fifth place is another scene in an established contender’s campaign. These are public standings; the private finish still lies ahead.

So who is underneath the stage lights? Pull up a chair.

sections.heading: Florian Sestak: silverware, school exams and a long apprenticeship
sections.text:
The fses91 handle belongs to Florian Sestak. His Kaggle profile links straight to the GitHub account carrying his full name. Our earlier notebook knew him only as Florian; that missing surname is now settled.

Sestak has a proper competition scrapbook. His completed-results page records silver for thirty-eighth of 4,463 in the Santander Value Prediction Challenge, plus bronze finishes in NFL Helmet Assignment, Jigsaw Unintended Bias and Porto Seguro’s Safe Driver Prediction. The Jigsaw result belongs to a shared entry. His record also includes ARC Prize 2025. This is a return to the arena with years of experience behind him.

The old discussions supply the personality. In January 2018 he was openly asking why competitors transformed their prediction targets. By April 2019, he was telling fellow Santander contestants that his approach had taken him into the gold ranks before exams interrupted his campaign. When he returned, he wrestled with the gap between his own validation results and the leaderboard, and thanked people whose notebooks improved his skills even when they did not improve his placing. The questions, the frustration, the generosity: you can follow the apprenticeship in his own posts.

This season brought a different sort of exam. Before the first ARC3 milestone, Sestak publicly described holding a top-three position for four days with nine submissions, then slipping to fourth. His supervisor, Günter Klambauer, proudly amplified the account. Before the second milestone, Sestak announced he was back among the top ten. On October 11, he was in the Kaggle forum helping another competitor find the grid-and-action documentation.

Away from the board, his own career record runs from data science at Siemens and 7LYTIX to doctoral research at JKU. His research works with generative models for biology and physics; the LaM-SLidE paper gives that work a public face. There is a lot of mileage behind the black cap and sunglasses.

sections.heading: Lukas Aichberger: he was competing with robots before this dance
sections.text:
Lukas Aichberger’s contest story reaches back well before the present LLM race. He and Florian Müller represented Austria in Mobile Robotics at EuroSkills 2016, finishing fifth in the official results. Their school had celebrated the pair as national runners-up. That is a different Florian from teammate Florian Sestak—and a very different arena from Kaggle—but the competitive streak is on the record.

Since then, Aichberger has built a research career around making AI reason efficiently and recognise when it might be wrong. His own biography says he completed his AI doctorate through the ELLIS programme, co-supervised by Sepp Hochreiter and Yarin Gal, worked with Oxford’s OATML group, and worked on reasoning and post-training at Apple. That is quite a route from the mobile-robotics floor to the scoring hall.

His 2026 paper with Hochreiter, Reasoning in Memory, asks whether a language model can work through a problem in an internal workspace instead of spelling out every intermediate thought. It is an appealing idea for anyone watching agents spend their time thinking—but the paper is a research achievement, not a disclosure of The Last Dance’s competition recipe.

For our recurring cast, Lukas keeps the swept brown hair and friendly, clean-shaven face of his own Kaggle cartoon. We have given him an ARC-grid hoodie and the middle of the dance floor. His public research profile invites ambitious collaborations in reasoning, post-training and agent safety. There is a next chapter taking shape beyond this competition, too.

sections.heading: Mykyta Ielanskyi: the bearded puzzle man already has an award
sections.text:
The dwellement0baser account is Mykyta Ielanskyi, whose Kaggle profile identifies him as a research scientist at JKU’s Institute for Machine Learning. His earlier competition history includes a team appearance in Kaggriculture. But the trophy worth bringing into this introduction comes from his reasoning research.

Ielanskyi was one of the six authors honoured with an Outstanding Paper Award at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on Logical Reasoning of Large Language Models. The paper, From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles, connects a language model’s reading ability with a symbolic solver’s exact reasoning. JKU records the award on April 23; TU Wien’s announcement names the whole winning group. Give the man his applause.

His connection with Lukas is older than this campaign. Both appear on the 2023 NeurIPS paper Quantification of Uncertainty with Adversarial Models, alongside Kajetan Schweighofer, Günter Klambauer and Hochreiter. In June 2026, Ielanskyi was first author of RREDCoT, again working with Schweighofer, Aichberger and Hochreiter. That paper investigates how to reward useful portions of a model’s reasoning instead of judging only the eventual answer.

The sporting attraction is obvious: this is someone who spends his research life asking how machines reason, where they go wrong and how to make the process better. TU Wien’s biography places uncertainty, post-training, decoding and life-science applications among his interests. In our illustration, his own tousled hair and full reddish beard stay unmistakable under the cyan-and-green ARC suit.

sections.heading: The professor in the orbit—and what comes after the next submission
sections.text:
There is a professor with form in this story. Günter Klambauer is Sestak’s named supervisor and a collaborator of both Lukas and Mykyta. JKU credits his research with self-normalizing neural networks, xLSTM and machine learning for the life sciences. His scientific competition record includes the winning Bioinf@JKU teams in the 2014 Tox21 challenge and a best-performing method in the 2013 DREAM Toxicogenetics challenge. The encouragement he gave Sestak came from someone who knows what a scientific contest feels like.

One identification remains open: the roster’s gklambauer account supplies no real name or personal portrait. Its two public Kaggle comments correct descriptions of self-normalization in an older notebook. The handle and research connections make the professor an obvious lead, but we have not found a direct account link that confirms he owns it. We therefore keep the fourth member under that handle and use a deliberately fictional masked dancer, not Kaggle’s generic goose or a borrowed human face.

What are they doing next? The public trail is busy. Sestak is a coauthor of Bi-FORK, released on October 8, on modelling physical systems with several possible outcomes. Aichberger is pursuing efficient reasoning and robust agents. Ielanskyi’s recent work tackles reasoning, rewards and exact puzzle solving. In their wider research circle, Klambauer coauthored the October 19 KronLSTM paper on long-context memory. These are real projects readers can follow; none establishes what is inside the team’s current ARC3 agent.

For the competition, the delicious unanswered question is what The Last Dance has left for the finish. The reviewed public discussions do not reveal its next submission or a promised release date. We do have a four-account contender that has twice reached third in the saved October record, now defending fifth while the pack closes behind it. The name says last dance. The board says the music is still playing.
